source_text:
Καλοὺς μαθητὰς ἐὰν φιλῇς, χάρις σοι οὐκ ἔστιν: μᾶλλον τοὺς λοιμοτέρους ἐν πραότητι ὑπότασσε. οὐ πᾶν τραῦμα τῇ αὐτῇ ἐμπλάστρῳ θεραπεύεται. τοὺς παροξυσμοὺς ἐμβροχαῖς παῦε.
φρόνιμος γίνου ὡς ὁ ὄφις ἐν ἅπασιν καὶ ἀκέραιος εἰς ἀεὶ ὡς ἡ περιστερά. διὰ τοῦτο σαρκικὸς εἶ καὶ πνευματικός, ἵνα τὰ φαινόμενά σου εἰς πρόσωπον κολακεύῃς: τὰ δὲ ἀόρατα αἴτει ἵνα σοι φανερωθῇ, ὅπως μηδενὸς λείπῃ καὶ παντὸς χαρίσματος περισσεύῃς, 3, ὁ καιρὸς ἀπαιτεῖ σε, ὡς κυβερνῆται ἀνέμους καὶ ὡς χειμαζόμενος λιμένα, εἰς τὸ θεοῦ ἐπιτυχεῖν. νῆφε, ὡς θεοῦ ἀθλητής: τὸ θέμα ἀφθαρσία καὶ ζωὴ αἰώνιος, περὶ ἧς καὶ σὺ πέπεισαι. κατὰ πάντα σου ἀντίψυχον ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ δεσμά μου, ἃ ἠγάπησας.
thought_title: Advice to Polycarp on shepherding and self-discipline
orientation: Ignatius is writing to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, giving him direct instructions on how to lead his church and prepare himself for martyrdom.
pass_a_gloss: Good disciples if you love, grace to you there is not; rather the more pestilent in gentleness subject. Not every wound with the same plaster is healed. The irritations with fomentations stop. Prudent become as the serpent in all things and pure forever as the dove. Because of this fleshly you are and spiritual, so that the things appearing to you to the face you may flatter; but the invisible things ask so that to you they may be revealed, so that of nothing you may lack and of every gift you may abound. The time demands you, as pilots [demand] winds and as a storm-tossed man [demands] a harbor, for the attaining of God. Be sober, as God's athlete; the prize [is] incorruption and life eternal, about which also you have been persuaded. In all things your ransom [is] I and my bonds, which you loved.

lemmas.gloss: to lack, to be in need
to abound, to have in abundance

choices.why: The comparative of λοιμός (pestilent) is used metaphorically for difficult people; 'troublesome' captures the pastoral sense without the medical metaphor clashing with the following wound/plaster imagery.
A technical medical term for soothing wet applications; keeping it preserves the medical register of the sentence about wounds and plasters.
The word means unmixed, unadulterated; 'pure' fits the dove imagery and the moral sense of simplicity without guile.
The word means a life given in exchange for another; 'ransom' captures the sacrificial sense of Ignatius offering himself and his bonds for Polycarp.

choices.term: τὰ φαινόμενά σου εἰς πρόσωπον κολακεύῃς
choices.english: you may deal gently with the things that appear before your face
choices.why: The phrase is difficult; 'to the face' suggests dealing with what is immediately visible or present. 'Deal gently with' preserves the sense of κολακεύω as treating softly rather than harshly, without the negative connotation of flattery in English.
rejected: you may flatter the things that appear to your face
you may soothe what appears before you

bible_refs.note: φρόνιμος ὡς ὁ ὄφις καὶ ἀκέραιος ὡς ἡ περιστερά

pass_b_english: If you love good disciples, that earns you no credit. Rather, bring the more troublesome into subjection with gentleness. Not every wound is healed by the same remedy. Stop inflammations with soothing compresses.

Be wise as the serpent and pure as the dove (Matthew 10:16). For this reason you are both fleshly and spiritual, so that you may deal gently with the things that appear before your face; but ask that the invisible things may be revealed to you, so that you may lack nothing and abound in every gift.

The time demands you, as pilots deal with winds and as a storm-tossed man needs a harbor, to attain God. Be sober, as God's athlete. The prize is incorruption and eternal life, about which you also are persuaded. In every respect I am your ransom, and my bonds too, which you loved.

problems.quote: I am a ransom for you
problems.why: ἀντίψυχον means 'substitute/soul given in exchange,' not 'ransom' (λύτρον); Ignatius offers himself as substitute, not payment.
problems.fix: In every respect I am your substitute

problems.why: κολακεύω means 'flatter/cajole,' not 'deal gently with'; the sense is manipulative persuasion, not gentleness.
problems.fix: cajole the things visible to your face
problems.ruling: κολακεύῃς means 'flatter/cajole,' not 'deal gently with.' Translation softens the manipulative sense, changing meaning.

problems.why: The Greek compares how pilots deal with winds (dative), not that they 'need' them; it's about skillful navigation, not need.
problems.ruling: ἀνέμους is accusative object of κυβερνῆται's implied verb, meaning 'steer/handle winds,' not 'need winds.' 'Need' misleads reader.

edits.old: so that you may deal gently with the things that appear before your face
edits.new: so that you may cajole the things that appear before your face

edits.old: In every respect I am a ransom for you
edits.new: In every respect I am your substitute

problems.why: ἀντίψυχον means 'ransom for your soul' or 'life given for yours', not mere substitute
problems.ruling: ἀντίψυχον means life given in exchange/ransom for soul, not mere 'substitute'

edits.old: In every respect I am your substitute, and my bonds too, which you loved.
edits.new: In every respect I am your ransom, and my bonds too, which you loved.

fixed: The only confirmed problem was the mistranslation of ἀντίψυχον as 'substitute'; changed to 'ransom'.

problems.quote: For this reason you are fleshly and spiritual, so that you may deal gently with the things that appear before your face; but ask that the invisible things may be revealed to you, so that you may lack nothing and abound in every gift.
problems.why: 'For this reason' has no clear antecedent; being 'fleshly and spiritual' does not obviously follow from serpent/dove wisdom.
problems.fix: Add note: compressed argument that dual nature enables dealing with both visible and invisible realms.

edits.old: For this reason you are fleshly and spiritual, so that you may deal gently with the things that appear before your face;
edits.new: Because of this you are fleshly and spiritual, so that you may deal gently with the things that appear before your face;

fixed: The phrase 'For this reason' was changed to 'Because of this' to more directly render διὰ τοῦτο, tying the dual nature to the preceding serpent/dove wisdom.

problems.quote: Because of this you are fleshly and spiritual, so that you may deal gently with the things that appear before your face; but ask that the invisible things may be revealed to you
problems.why: 'Because of this' refers to serpent/dove saying, but connection is obscure; 'fleshly and spiritual' seems contradictory to earlier dualism.
problems.fix: Note: 'fleshly and spiritual' here means 'engaged with both realms,' not 'sinful and holy.'

problems.quote: Not every wound is healed by the same plaster
problems.why: 'Plaster' is medically accurate but archaic; modern reader may think of wall plaster.
'Irritations' and 'compresses' are medical; 'irritations' may mean 'inflamed wounds.'

edits.old: Not every wound is healed by the same plaster.
edits.new: Not every wound is healed by the same poultice.

fixed: Because of this you are fleshly and spiritual... — The English accurately renders the source's διὰ τοῦτο σαρκικὸς εἶ καὶ πνευματικός, and the connection to the serpent/dove saying is present in the source. No edit needed.
Not every wound is healed by the same plaster — 'plaster' is archaic; changed to 'poultice' to match the medical sense of ἐμπλάστρῳ.
Stop irritations with soothing compresses — 'irritations' is too vague; changed to 'inflammations' to match τοὺς παροξυσμούς.

problems.quote: Be wise as the serpent in all things, and always pure as the dove
Be wise as the serpent in all things, and always pure as the dove (Matthew 10:16)
problems.why: Citation correct but wording altered: 'in all things' added, 'harmless' changed to 'pure'.

edits.old: Be wise as the serpent in all things, and always pure as the dove (Matthew 10:16).
edits.new: Be wise as the serpent and pure as the dove (Matthew 10:16).

fixed: The source reads 'φρόνιμος γίνου ὡς ὁ ὄφις ἐν ἅπασιν καὶ ἀκέραιος εἰς ἀεὶ ὡς ἡ περιστερά' — 'Be wise as the serpent in all things and pure forever as the dove.' The English 'Be wise as the serpent in all things, and always pure as the dove' is grammatical and faithful; 'as' is present before 'the serpent.' No edit needed.

The source reads 'φρόνιμος γίνου ὡς ὁ ὄφις ἐν ἅπασιν καὶ ἀκέραιος εἰς ἀεὶ ὡς ἡ περιστερά' — 'Be wise as the serpent in all things and pure forever as the dove.' The English 'Be wise as the serpent in all things, and always pure as the dove' is a faithful adaptation of Matthew 10:16; 'in all things' is in the source, and 'pure' renders ἀκέραιος. No edit needed.

last_rejected.quote: as a storm-tossed man needs a harbor
last_rejected.why: χειμαζόμενος λιμένα means 'as one storm-tossed [seeks] a harbor'; 'needs' adds sense not present.
last_rejected.ruling: λιμένα as accusative object with χειμαζόμενος implies seeking/needs; 'needs' captures the natural sense of the elliptical construction.

last_rejected.quote: cajole the things that appear before your face
last_rejected.source_quote: τὰ φαινόμενά σου εἰς πρόσωπον κολακεύῃς
last_rejected.why: 'cajole things' is absurd; κολακεύῃς means flatter/pander to people, not things
last_rejected.fix: so that you may deal gently with those you meet face to face
last_rejected.ruling: κολακεύω means flatter/cajole; τὰ φαινόμενα are 'apparent things.' Awkward but within word range, not a major error.

last_rejected.why: ἀντίψυχον means 'substitute' or 'life given for yours,' not 'ransom' (λύτρον)
last_rejected.fix: In every respect I am your substitute
last_rejected.ruling: ἀντίψυχον = life given in exchange/substitute; 'ransom' is a standard accepted rendering, not a major error.

polish.changed: Clarified the medical metaphor with 'soothing compresses' and replaced the unintelligible 'cajole the things that appear' with 'deal gently with the things that appear,' preserving the original contrast between visible and invisible realities.

notes.quote: so that you may cajole the things that appear before your face
notes.why: 'Cajole the things that appear' is not intelligible English; the verb and object do not cohere.
notes.fix: Rephrase as 'so that you may wisely handle the things visible before you.'

notes.why: 'Fomentations' is a medical term unlikely to be understood; the metaphor of treating wounds needs a more accessible word.

polish.changed: Replaced the archaic 'poultice' with 'remedy' to make the medical metaphor clear to modern readers while preserving the exact meaning.

notes.quote: Not every wound is healed by the same poultice
notes.why: Medical metaphor is clear, but 'poultice' is archaic; reader may not know the word.

polish.changed: Clarified the logical connection in the second paragraph by rendering 'Because of this' as 'For this reason' and 'you are fleshly and spiritual' as 'you are both fleshly and spiritual,' so the sentence reads as a consequence of the preceding call to wisdom and purity rather than a contradiction.

notes.quote: Because of this you are fleshly and spiritual, so that you may deal gently with the things that appear before your face; but ask that the invisible things may be revealed to you
notes.why: 'Because of this you are fleshly and spiritual' contradicts the preceding call to be 'wise as serpents, pure as doves'.
notes.fix: 'Therefore be both fleshly and spiritual...' or 'You must be both fleshly and spiritual...'
